Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
Marlene Kowalski is a 58-year-old widowed woman of Polish-American heritage who presents to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 75, seeking help for symptoms she has been carrying, largely in silence, for several years. She is currently unemployed, having left her last position some time ago under circumstances she connects, in her own quiet way, to what happened to her son.

The event that fractured Marlene's life occurred on a late autumn afternoon when her son, then 27, was struck by a car at an intersection not far from her home. Marlene did not witness the collision itself, but she arrived at the scene within minutes of being called — before the ambulance had left, before the road had been cleared. What she found when she stepped out of her car was the particular stillness of her son on the asphalt, the smell of engine fluid and something metallic that she has never been able to name, and the sight of his car pushed sideways against a concrete barrier, the driver's door caved inward. Her son survived, but sustained injuries that required months of hospitalisation and left him with lasting physical limitations. Marlene spent those months at his bedside, and in the years since she has told herself that he recovered, that it was not the worst outcome, and that she has no right to be the one who is struggling.

That reasoning has not made the symptoms easier to bear. The smell she encountered at the scene returns to her without invitation — she will be sitting in her kitchen or walking through a parking garage and suddenly the odour is there, not as a memory she has chosen to revisit but as something present and immediate, pulling her back to the asphalt. What frightens her most about these moments is their completeness: something in her surroundings — the glint of a damaged car door in a parking lot, the blue flash of ambulance lights at the end of a street — can collapse the distance between then and now entirely, and she is no longer a woman standing in an ordinary place but someone standing over her son again. She has come to believe that these intrusions arrive without any logic she can predict or control, which means that nowhere feels entirely safe.

At the same time, when Marlene has tried to sit down and deliberately recall the sequence of events — to tell herself the story in order, the way she imagines a person ought to be able to do — the memory resists her. It comes in fragments, out of sequence, or not at all. She finds this deeply unsettling, as though something essential has been taken from her.

In the months and years following the accident, Marlene began organising her life around the edges of what she could not tolerate. She stopped driving past the intersection. She changed the route she walked to the pharmacy so that she would not pass a stretch of road where she had once seen an ambulance idling. She had been working part-time as a receptionist at a medical office when, during a shift, an ambulance pulled into the adjacent bay and she found herself unable to return to her desk. She did not go back to that job. Now she rarely leaves the house on the anniversary of the accident, spending the day in a state of dread that begins building days in advance.

At home, Marlene checks the locks on her doors and windows repeatedly before she can attempt sleep — a ritual that has lengthened over time without her fully noticing. She startles badly at unexpected movement, the neighbour's dog appearing suddenly at the fence, a grandchild running into the room, and she is ashamed of the way her body reacts as though each of these is a threat. Sleep comes reluctantly and does not hold.

What finally brought Marlene to seek help was her son himself, who told her gently that he had watched her shrink. She came to the first session hoping, above all, to understand why she cannot simply remember what happened and move past it — and afraid, in equal measure, that the answer will confirm what she has quietly suspected: that something in her is permanently broken.
